newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's new PM faces daunting economic task.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's new PM faces daunting economic task.

text.p: Nawaz Sharif's stunning election victory has ended months of political uncertainty, but Pakistan's prime minister-elect faces a stern challenge in bringing the economy back on track, analysts said on Sunday.

"The recent stock market recovery was sentiment-driven and it is more or less over. Any further rise will depend on actual performance and tangible results," said Jahanzeb Naseer, head of research at Jardine Fleming Pakistan Broking.

Sharif, due to be sworn in on Monday after sweeping back to power in the February 3 elections, inherits from a caretaker government rising inflation, a worsening balance of payments, a crushing foreign debt burden and low foreign exchange reserves.
"The current fiscal year is proving to be very difficult, with negative trends reflected in most economic indicators," analyst Zuna Mansoor of ING Baring Securities said.
The consumer price index rose 2.17 percent in January over December, a year-on-year increase of 13.4 percent, up from 11.41 percent in December and 8.93 percent in January 1996.
The trade gap rose to a provisional $2.126 billion in the first seven months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from $2.097 billion in the year-ago period.
Foreign exchange reserves, excluding gold, plummeted to $598 million on February 6 from $680 million on January 30.

"In current circumstances, striking a deal with the International Monetary Fund for an enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) appears to be Pakistan's best option," Naseer said. Previous economic managers had already scraped the barrel for short-term financing, he added.

A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said the current account deficit was likely to shoot beyond $5.0 billion in 1996/97 (July-June) with foreign debt servicing reaching $2.25 billion and an estimated trade deficit of $2.8 billion.
"The main issue with the IMF is that of containing the budget deficit within four percent of Gross Domestic Product from 6.3 percent in 1995/96," Naseer said.
He said the target would be hard to reach given the inelastic nature of the spending side of the equation.
"Annual expenditures on defence and debt servicing combined account for more than total net revenues and nearly 70 percent of gross revenues," he said.
Naseer said the government would be wise to introduce reforms on the revenue side and improve documentation of Pakistan's economy, much of which is informal.

"Either you go for more foreign and domestic borrowing, higher taxes and devaluation to boost export earnings, or you go for revenue-generation measures which can bring the shadowy economy into the tax net," he said.

Given Sharif's industry-friendly credentials, Naseer said he expected some additional tax on agriculture. An ESAF programme worth $2.0 to $2.5 billion would give the government a breathing space to implement structural changes on the revenue side.

Analyst Munir Ladha of AKD Securities said that in view of Sharif's massive mandate, the IMF was likely to allow him some room to ease the targets and negotiate a fresh ESAF with a practical implementation plan later this year.

"Speedy privatisation, a steady inflow of foreign exchange from expatriates and other investors amid lowering of political risk attached to investments in Pakistan is likely to make Sharif's job a bit easier than his predecessor's," Ladha said.
Kalim Aziz, research head at ING Baring Securities, said Sharif, strong on the supply side of the economy, was likely to focus on stimulating production, exports and consumption.
